claim: The equilibrium distributions for organelle numbers predicted by the stochastic model of organelle production can be readily calculated in three different scenarios.
source: We present a reanalysis of the stochastic model of organelle production and show that the equilibrium distributions for the organelle numbers predicted by this model can be readily calculated in three different scenarios.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mathematical derivations and calculations presented throughout the manuscript, including recurrence relations and exact formulae.

claim: The three equilibrium distributions can be identified as standard distributions.
source: These three distributions can be identified as standard distributions, and the corresponding exact formulae for their mean and variance can therefore be used in further analysis.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the distributions as Poisson (for Golgi), truncated Poisson (for vacuoles), and negative binomial (for peroxisomes).

claim: Using exact distributions removes the need to rely on stochastic simulations or approximate formulae derived using the fluctuation dissipation theorem.
source: This removes the need to rely on stochastic simulations or approximate formulae (derived using the fluctuation dissipation theorem).
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates that exact calculations can be performed using recurrence relations instead of simulations or approximations.

claim: The extent to which the model can conclude that peroxisome biogenesis is dominated by de novo production when Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells are grown on glucose medium is questionable.
source: On the basis of this we question the extent to which the model can be used to conclude that peroxisome biogenesis is dominated by de novo production when Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells are grown on glucose medium.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis showing that the interpretation of the original SMOP model regarding dominance of de novo production is misleading.

claim: A model was presented in which the variation of numbers of a particular type of organelle observed in cells was proposed as a diagnostic indicator of the relative importance of different processes by which organelles can be formed and destroyed.
source: Recently a model was presented in which the variation of numbers of a particular type of organelle (Golgi apparatus, vacuoles or peroxisomes) observed in cells was proposed as a diagnostic indicator of the relative importance of different processes by which organelles can be formed and destroyed (Mukherji and O'Shea, 2014; see Mukherji and O'Shea, 2015 for a correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original SMOP paper.

claim: In the SMOP model, four processes are envisaged for the production and destruction of organelles: de novo synthesis, fission, fusion and decay.
source: In the SMOP model, four processes are envisaged for the production and destruction of organelles: de novo synthesis, fission, fusion and decay.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure as presented in the original SMOP paper.

claim: Models involving birth and death processes have a very long history of analysis in the context of life sciences and physical processes.
source: Models involving processes of this type are generically termed "birth and death" processes and have a very long history of analysis in the context both of the life sciences (e.g. evolution; Yule, 1924) and in the context of physical processes (e.g. detection of cosmic rays; Furry, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical work by Yule (1924) and Furry (1937).

claim: In birth and death analyses, de novo production, production by fission, and loss by first order decay are often termed immigration, birth and death, respectively.
source: In such analyses, the three processes of de novo production, production by fission, and loss by first order decay are often termed immigration, birth and death, respectively.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field of birth and death processes.

claim: Immigration is used for a process that increases the number of individuals but does not require any other individuals already to be present.
source: Immigration is used for a process that increases the number of individuals but does not require any other individuals already to be present.
evidence: This is a standard definition in birth and death process theory.

claim: Birth is the process by which one individual gives rise to a second individual.
source: Birth is the process by which one individual gives rise to a second individual.
evidence: This is a standard definition in birth and death process theory.

claim: Death is a process by which a particular individual is lost from a population with a probability that is independent of any other members of the population.
source: Death is a process by which a particular individual is lost from a population with a probability that is independent of any other members of the population.
evidence: This is a standard definition in birth and death process theory.

claim: Analyses including a fusion term are much less common in birth and death models.
source: Analyses including a fusion term are much less common.
evidence: This is an observation about the literature on birth and death processes.

claim: In many birth and death models the system will settle down to a limiting distribution, independent of the starting states of the cell(s).
source: However in many birth and death models the system will settle down to a limiting distribution, independent of the starting states of the cell(s) as in the cyan and red curves in Figure 1C.
evidence: This is supported by both theoretical knowledge and the simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A limiting distribution corresponds to a state of dynamic equilibrium that is familiar from chemical kinetics.
source: Such a situation corresponds to a state of dynamic equilibrium that is familiar from chemical kinetics.
evidence: This draws on established knowledge from chemical kinetics.

claim: The terms limiting, equilibrium, and steady state distributions can be used interchangeably in this context.
source: Thus the terms limiting, equilibrium (or steady state) distributions can be used in this context interchangeably.
evidence: This is a statement about terminology in the field.

claim: It is implicitly assumed in the SMOP paper that the populations are to be considered to be at equilibrium for all three cases of the analysis.
source: It is implicitly assumed in the SMOP paper that the populations are to be considered to be at equilibrium (or that the probability distributions are in their limiting form) for all three cases of the analysis via simulations, from experimental data, or via the fluctuation dissipation theorem; a comment has been added to the original articles to clarify this assumption for the simulations (see the comment dated November 23, 2015 on Mukherji and O'Shea, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a comment added to the original SMOP paper.

claim: The fluctuation dissipation theorem method implicitly assumes a steady state.
source: The fluctuation dissipation theorem method implicitly assumes a steady state (Paulsson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paulsson (2005).

claim: At equilibrium, the rate at which the population gains cells with n + 1 organelles due to cells with n organelles gaining one organelle must equal the rate at which the cells with n + 1 organelles lose one organelle.
source: At equilibrium, the rate at which the population gains cells with n + 1 organelles due to cells with n organelles gaining one organelle must equal the rate at which the cells with n + 1 organelles lose one organelle.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of dynamic equilibrium applied to this system.

claim: The recurrence relation allows the exact distribution of organelle numbers at equilibrium to be calculated for a model involving any combination of the four processes, without recourse to random number based simulations.
source: From Equation 2 the exact distribution of organelle numbers at equilibrium can be calculated for a model involving any combination of the four processes, without recourse to random number based simulations and the attendant issues of ensuring adequate sampling precision.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical derivation and application of Equation 2.

claim: For the Golgi model ({de novo; decay}), a Poisson distribution is obtained as the limiting distribution in accord with the SMOP analysis.
source: For the Golgi, a Poisson distribution is obtained as the limiting distribution in accord with the SMOP analysis.
evidence: This is derived in Appendix 3 and agrees with the original SMOP analysis.

claim: For vacuoles, a truncated Poisson distribution is obtained, and not the shifted Poisson distribution that is reported in the SMOP analysis.
source: However for vacuoles a truncated Poisson distribution is obtained, and not the shifted Poisson distribution that is reported in the SMOP analysis.
evidence: This is derived in Appendix 4 and contradicts the original SMOP analysis.

claim: The Fano factor for the truncated Poisson approaches 1 much more rapidly than for the shifted Poisson.
source: the Fano factor for the truncated Poisson approaches 1 much more rapidly (Figure 2, green curve) than for the shifted Poisson (Figure 2, black curve).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the curves shown in Figure 2.

claim: The experimental values for vacuoles quoted in the SMOP analysis are in excellent agreement with the incorrect prediction (shifted Poisson), whilst the agreement with the corrected theoretical prediction (truncated Poisson) is much less good.
source: In Figure 2, it can be seen that the experimental values quoted in the SMOP analysis are in excellent agreement with the incorrect prediction, whilst the agreement with the corrected theoretical prediction is much less good.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the experimental data points with the theoretical curves in Figure 2.

claim: The corrected analysis greatly weakens the argument that the SMOP model makes quantitatively accurate predictions for vacuoles.
source: This greatly weakens the argument that the SMOP model makes "quantitatively accurate predictions" or that it therefore correctly accounts for the behaviour of the vacuole population.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor agreement between corrected predictions and experimental data.

claim: The {de novo, fission; decay} model has a limiting distribution that is a negative binomial distribution.
source: We show in Appendix 5 that such a {de novo, fission; decay} model has a limiting distribution that is a negative binomial distribution.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in Appendix 5.

claim: The expression σ²/n = 1 + kfission<n>/kde novo is exact for all values of the parameters when kfusion = 0.
source: By explicitly applying the equilibrium assumption we have therefore shown that this expression is exact in this case for all values of the parameters.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical derivation.

claim: The inferred fission rate for growth on oleate is only barely greater than the de novo synthesis rate.
source: In the corrected version of Figure 3D in the SMOP paper it is clear that the inferred fission rate for growth on oleate is only barely greater than the de novo synthesis rate and the term "dominance" does not seem to be appropriate.
evidence: This is inferred from the corrected analysis of the Fano factor data.

claim: The inferred contribution from fission grows only rather slowly as the Fano factor increases above a value of two.
source: It is clear from Figure 3 that the inferred contribution from fission grows only rather slowly as the Fano factor increases above a value of two.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For fission to be truly dominant, a Fano factor would have to be observed that was far greater than any reported in the SMOP paper.
source: In other words, for fission to be truly dominant a Fano factor would have to be observed that was far greater than any reported in the SMOP paper.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of how the Fano factor relates to the relative contributions of fission and de novo production.

claim: For the {de novo, fission; decay} model to have a limiting or equilibrium distribution, kfission must be less than γ.
source: In the case of the peroxisome model, {de novo, fission; decay}, for the system to have a limiting or equilibrium distribution there is a strong restriction on parameters, namely that kfission < γ.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the conditions for convergence of the distribution.

claim: If kfission exceeds γ then the fission process will always exceed the decay process and the number of organelles will grow without limit.
source: If kfission exceeds γ then the fission process will always exceed the decay process and the number of organelles will grow without limit.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the rate equations and is demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The agreement of experimental data with the SMOP model is not as compelling as originally presented.
source: This means that the agreement of experimental data with the model is not as compelling as originally presented and that the interpretation of experimental observations back to mechanistic conclusions is open to question.
evidence: This is inferred from the corrected analysis showing poorer agreement with experimental data.

claim: A key conclusion of the SMOP analysis is that the contribution of fission to peroxisome biogenesis is negligible (<10%) when yeast cells are grown on glucose.
source: A key conclusion of the SMOP analysis is that the contribution of fission to peroxisome biogenesis is negligible (<10%) when yeast cells are grown on glucose, but "dominant" when they are grown on oleate.
evidence: This summarizes a conclusion from the original SMOP paper.

claim: The contribution of fission to peroxisome biogenesis is dominant when yeast cells are grown on oleate according to the SMOP analysis.
source: A key conclusion of the SMOP analysis is that the contribution of fission to peroxisome biogenesis is negligible (<10%) when yeast cells are grown on glucose, but "dominant" when they are grown on oleate.
evidence: This summarizes a conclusion from the original SMOP paper.

claim: The mechanism of peroxisome biogenesis is an area of some contention.
source: This is an area of some contention (Hoepfner et al, 2005; Motley and Hettema, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers with differing views.

claim: A recent model relied on fission of peroxisomes during organelle inheritance as the proliferation mechanism.
source: and a recent model relied on fission of peroxisomes during organelle inheritance as the proliferation mechanism (Knoblach et al, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Knoblach et al. (2013).

claim: The term 'dominant' is misleading when describing the contribution of fission to peroxisome biogenesis on oleate.
source: Our analysis has shown that the term "dominant" is misleading, and that the data reported for haploid cells grown on oleate indicates approximately equal contributions from the two processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the corrected analysis of the Fano factor.

claim: The data reported for haploid cells grown on oleate indicates approximately equal contributions from de novo and fission processes.
source: Our analysis has shown that the term "dominant" is misleading, and that the data reported for haploid cells grown on oleate indicates approximately equal contributions from the two processes.
evidence: This is calculated from the corrected analysis using the exact formulae.

claim: The model suggests that the proportion of production by fission increases by about a factor of five on switching to oleate growth.
source: Nevertheless the model does suggest that the proportion of production by fission increases by about a factor of five on switching to oleate growth.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the model predictions for glucose and oleate conditions.

claim: Supporting evidence for increased fission on oleate was provided by the observation of the reduction in the inferred fission contribution in cells grown on oleate in which the fission factors Vps1 or Dnm1 (or Fis1) were deleted.
source: Supporting evidence for this was provided by the observation of the reduction in the inferred fission contribution in cells grown on oleate in which the fission factors Vps1 or Dnm1 (or Fis1, an accessory factor of Dnm1) were deleted.
evidence: This refers to experimental data from the original SMOP paper.

claim: No data were shown for glucose grown cells harbouring deletions of Vps1, Dnm1, or Fis1 in the SMOP paper.
source: On the other hand, no data were shown for glucose grown cells harbouring the same deletions.
evidence: This is an observation about what was reported in the original SMOP paper.

claim: On glucose, the Fano factor is reported in the SMOP analysis as 1.1, with <n> = 3.
source: On glucose the Fano factor is reported in the SMOP analysis as 1.1, with <n> = 3
evidence: This cites data from the original SMOP paper.

claim: From the SMOP model parameters for glucose growth, kde novo = 2.7γ and kfission = 0.1γ.
source: and from Equations 3,4 one obtains kde novo = 2.7γ and kfission = 0.1γ.
evidence: This is calculated from Equations 3 and 4 using the reported Fano factor and mean.

claim: The SMOP model implies that on deletion of the fission pathway (setting kfission = 0) on glucose, <n> would only drop by 10%.
source: The model then implies that on deletion of the fission pathway (i.e. setting kfission = 0) then <n> would only drop by 10%.
evidence: This is calculated from the model equations with the inferred parameters.

claim: Peroxisome count data reported by Motley et al. (2015) shows <n> = 4.9 in WT cells, <n> = 1.5 in vps1Δ cells and <n> = 1.2 in vps1Δdnm1Δ cells.
source: Peroxisome count data has been reported recently (Fig S4, Motley et al., 2015), with values of <n> = 4.9 in WT cells, <n> = 1.5 in vps1Δ cells and <n> = 1.2 in vps1Δdnm1Δ cells.
evidence: This cites experimental data from Motley et al. (2015).

claim: The drops in peroxisome numbers in vps1Δ and vps1Δdnm1Δ cells are much greater than the 10% estimated from the SMOP model.
source: The drops in peroxisome numbers in vps1Δ and vps1Δdnm1Δ cells are much greater than the 10% estimated above from the SMOP model.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the experimental data from Motley et al. (2015) with the model prediction.

claim: Peroxisome count data from Kuravi et al. (2006) gives <n> = 1.6 (WT), <n> = 1.2 (vps1Δ), <n> = 1.7 (dnm1Δ), <n> = 0.9 (dnm1Δvps1Δ).
source: There is also peroxisome count data in Kuravi et al. (2006), which gives <n> = 1.6 (WT), <n> = 1.2 (vps1Δ), <n> = 1.7 (dnm1Δ), <n> = 0.9 (dnm1Δvps1Δ).
evidence: This cites experimental data from Kuravi et al. (2006).

claim: The drop in <n> for the dnm1Δvps1Δ strain conflicts with the idea that fission is such a small contributor to the biogenesis process on glucose.
source: The drop in <n> for the dnm1Δvps1Δ again conflicts with the idea that fission is such a small contributor to the biogenesis process.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing experimental data with model predictions.

claim: The discrepancies between various peroxisome count data possibly arise from difficulties in quantifying peroxisome numbers, especially when cells contain a large number of small peroxisomes.
source: The discrepancies between these various data possibly arise from difficulties in quantifying peroxisome numbers, especially when cells contain a large number of small (and therefore low fluorescence) peroxisomes as may be the case when fission is a strong contributor to biogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of discrepancies in the data.

claim: The problem of peroxisome counts depending on the brightness of fluorescent markers has been commented on by Jung et al. (2010).
source: The problem of peroxisome counts depending on the brightness of fluorescent markers has been commented on by Jung et al. (2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al. (2010).

claim: This work highlights the need for greater accounting for detection limits and intensity distributions in the reporting and analysis of organelle count data.
source: In particular this work highlights the need for greater accounting for detection limits and intensity distributions, as well of time dependent issues, in the reporting and analysis of organelle count data, if these are to be used to infer details of organelle biogenesis mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Time dependent issues need to be accounted for in the reporting and analysis of organelle count data if these are to be used to infer details of organelle biogenesis mechanisms.
source: In particular this work highlights the need for greater accounting for detection limits and intensity distributions, as well of time dependent issues, in the reporting and analysis of organelle count data, if these are to be used to infer details of organelle biogenesis mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simulations starting from different initial conditions (n=0 and n=50) both settle down to stochastic fluctuations about a mean value of <n> = 7.1.
source: (A) The traces show simulations run with the parameters {kde novo = 2.0, kfission = 0.9; γ = 1.0, kfusion = 0.02}, starting from n = 0 (black trace) and n = 50 (green trace). Both simulations "settle down" to stochastic fluctuations about a mean value of <n> = 7.1
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When kfission > γ and kfusion = 0, then n diverges and there is no limiting distribution.
source: (D) The red trace is a time course for parameters {kde novo = 2.0, kfission = 1.1; γ = 1.0, kfusion = 0}. Since kfission > γ, and kfusion = 0, then n diverges; in such a case there is no limiting distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Distributions calculated at different times after initialization (τ = 0.2, 0.4, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 15.0) show convergence to a limiting distribution.
source: (C) Distributions calculated with the same parameters as in (A) for a set of 1000 cells as in (B), calculated for τ = 0.2 (magenta), 0.4 (yellow), 1.0 (green), 2.0 (blue), 5.0 (black), 10.0 (cyan), 15.0 (red). The curves for τ = 10.0 and τ = 15.0 become very similar as they approach the limiting distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distributions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The curves for τ = 10.0 and τ = 15.0 match closely the result of applying the recurrence relation (Equation 2).
source: These two curves match closely the result (filled black circles) of applying the recurrence relation (Equation 2; Appendix 2).
evidence: This is shown by comparison in Figure 1C.

claim: The experimental values for vacuoles from haploid cells grown on glucose have a Fano factor around 0.52 and <n> around 2.0.
source: Three data points quoted in the SMOP paper are plotted: □ Haploid (glucose); ○ Diploid (glucose); ∆ Haploid (oleate).
evidence: This can be read from the position of the square symbol in Figure 2.

claim: The experimental values for vacuoles from diploid cells grown on glucose have a Fano factor around 0.70 and <n> around 3.0.
source: Three data points quoted in the SMOP paper are plotted: □ Haploid (glucose); ○ Diploid (glucose); ∆ Haploid (oleate).
evidence: This can be read from the position of the circle symbol in Figure 2.

claim: The experimental values for vacuoles from haploid cells grown on oleate have a Fano factor around 0.80 and <n> around 4.0.
source: Three data points quoted in the SMOP paper are plotted: □ Haploid (glucose); ○ Diploid (glucose); ∆ Haploid (oleate).
evidence: This can be read from the position of the triangle symbol in Figure 2.

claim: For a Fano factor of 1.1 (experimentally observed for glucose growth), the model predicts 9% de novo and 91% fission contribution.
source: Bars are shown for Fano factors of: 1.0 (100% de novo); 1.1 (experimentally observed for glucose growth (G) in SMOP paper; 9% de novo, 91% fission)
evidence: This is calculated using Equation 5 and shown in Figure 3.

claim: For a Fano factor of 2.4 (experimentally reported value for oleate growth), the model predicts 42% de novo and 58% fission contribution.
source: 2.4 (experimentally reported value for oleate growth (O) in SMOP paper; 42% de novo, 58% fission)
evidence: This is calculated using Equation 5 and shown in Figure 3.

claim: A Fano factor of 3.0 would be required for the fission rate to be double the de novo rate.
source: 3.0 (value required for fission rate to be double the de novo rate)
evidence: This is calculated using Equation 5 and shown in Figure 3.
